claim: Fragility fracture is associated with an increased risk of mortality.
source: Fragility fracture is associated with an increased risk of mortality, but mortality is not part of doctor-patient communication.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited throughout the manuscript and supported by data from the study.

claim: Mortality is not part of doctor-patient communication about fracture.
source: Fragility fracture is associated with an increased risk of mortality, but mortality is not part of doctor-patient communication.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in current clinical practice.

claim: Skeletal Age is defined as the sum of chronological age and the number of years of life lost (YLL) associated with a fracture.
source: Skeletal age is defined as the sum of chronological age and the number of years of life lost (YLL) associated with a fracture.
evidence: This is the operational definition provided in the abstract.

claim: The study included 1,667,339 adults in Denmark born on or before January 1, 1950.
source: We used the Danish National Hospital Discharge Register which includes the whole-country data of 1,667,339 adults in Denmark born on or before January 1, 1950, who were followed up to December 31, 2016 for incident low-trauma fracture and mortality.
evidence: This is the study population size reported in the methods.

claim: During the median follow-up period of 16 years, there had been 307,870 fractures and 122,744 post-fracture deaths.
source: During the median follow-up period of 16 years, there had been 307,870 fractures and 122,744 post-fracture deaths.
evidence: These are the primary outcome data from the study.

claim: A fracture was associated with between 1 and 7 years of life lost.
source: A fracture was associated with between 1 and 7 years of life lost, with the loss being greater in men than women.
evidence: This is a key finding from the analysis.

claim: The loss of years of life associated with fracture was greater in men than women.
source: A fracture was associated with between 1 and 7 years of life lost, with the loss being greater in men than women.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between sexes.

claim: Hip fractures incurred the greatest loss of life years.
source: Hip fractures incurred the greatest loss of life years.
evidence: This is a specific finding about hip fractures.

claim: A 60-year-old individual with a hip fracture is estimated to have a skeletal age of 66 for men and 65 for women.
source: For instance, a 60-year-old individual with a hip fracture is estimated to have a skeletal age of 66 for men and 65 for women.
evidence: This is a specific example calculation from the study.

claim: Fracture is a direct consequence of osteoporosis, just as stroke is a consequence of hypertension.
source: Fragility fracture is a direct consequence of osteoporosis, just as stroke is a consequence of hypertension.
evidence: This is an analogy used to explain the relationship between osteoporosis and fracture.

claim: Patients with a fragility fracture have on average a twofold increase in the risk of mortality.
source: Indeed, patients with a fragility fracture have on average a twofold increase in the risk of mortality (Center et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Between 22% and 58% of patients with a hip fracture die within 12 months post fracture.
source: Between 22% (Brauer et al., 2009) and 58% (Rapp et al., 2008) of patients with a hip fracture die within 12 months post fracture.
evidence: This is a range of mortality rates cited from previous studies.

claim: Treating high-risk individuals reduces the risk of fracture in randomized controlled trials.
source: In randomized controlled trials, treating high-risk individuals reduces the risk of fracture (Black et al., 2020), though whether the reduction translates into reduced mortality risk remains contentious (Bolland et al., 2010; Cummings et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a randomized controlled trial.

claim: Whether the reduction in fracture risk translates into reduced mortality risk remains contentious.
source: In randomized controlled trials, treating high-risk individuals reduces the risk of fracture (Black et al., 2020), though whether the reduction translates into reduced mortality risk remains contentious (Bolland et al., 2010; Cummings et al., 2019).
evidence: This is acknowledged as an area of ongoing debate with citations.

claim: Only 40% of hip fracture patients in the United States were given osteoporosis treatment within 1 month after discharge in 2002, which was then halved in 2011.
source: However, the treatment uptake has been low, with only 40% of hip fracture patients in the United States being given osteoporosis treatment within 1 month after discharge in 2002, which was then halved in 2011 (Solomon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a specific statistic about treatment uptake cited from previous research.

claim: Undertreatment of osteoporosis is considered a crisis in the management of osteoporosis globally.
source: This undertreatment is considered a crisis in the management of osteoporosis globally.
evidence: This is a characterization of the current state of osteoporosis management.

claim: Relative risk often gives an exaggerated impression.
source: Traditionally, relative risk (e.g. "the risk of mortality is increased by twofold") has been used as a metric of excess risk, but this metric often gives an exaggerated impression (Trevena et al., 2013), and is perceived as larger than the absolute risk (Akl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on risk communication.

claim: Relative risk is perceived as larger than the absolute risk.
source: Traditionally, relative risk (e.g. "the risk of mortality is increased by twofold") has been used as a metric of excess risk, but this metric often gives an exaggerated impression (Trevena et al., 2013), and is perceived as larger than the absolute risk (Akl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on risk perception.

claim: Absolute risk in terms of probability over a period of time is much harder to understand.
source: On the other hand, absolute risk in terms of probability over a period of time is much harder to understand (Zipkin et al., 2014), even for doctors and patients (Gigerenzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on risk comprehension.

claim: Only a fifth of a sample of highly educated American adults could understand one in 1000 is equivalent to 0.1%.
source: Only a fifth of a sample of highly educated American adults could understand one in 1000 is equivalent to 0.1% (Lipkus et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study on numeracy.

claim: In engineering, effective age is the age of a structure based on its current conditions.
source: In engineering, effective age is the age of a structure based on its current conditions; whereas in medicine, the effective age of an individual is the age of a typical healthy person who matches the specific risk profile of this individual (Spiegelhalter, 2016).
evidence: This is a definition cited from Spiegelhalter's work.

claim: In medicine, the effective age of an individual is the age of a typical healthy person who matches the specific risk profile of this individual.
source: In engineering, effective age is the age of a structure based on its current conditions; whereas in medicine, the effective age of an individual is the age of a typical healthy person who matches the specific risk profile of this individual (Spiegelhalter, 2016).
evidence: This is a definition cited from Spiegelhalter's work.

claim: The use of heart age and lung age has resulted in a better clinical impact than the traditional absolute risk metric.
source: The use of heart age and lung age has resulted in a better clinical impact than the traditional absolute risk metric (Kulendrarajah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on effective age metrics.

claim: The study included all adults aged 50 years old and older as of January 1, 2001 in Denmark.
source: This analysis included all adults aged 50 years old and older as of January 1, 2001 in Denmark whose health status had been followed up until December 31, 2016 for mortality.
evidence: This describes the study population inclusion criteria.

claim: Individuals who had sustained a fracture at 45+ years old between 1996 and 2000 were excluded to avoid potential bias that the incident fracture analyzed in this study was a second fracture.
source: Individuals who had sustained a fracture at 45+ years old between 1996 and 2000 were excluded to avoid potential bias that the incident fracture analyzed in this study was a second fracture (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an exclusion criterion explained in the methods and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The initial incident fracture was defined as the first low-trauma fracture reported between January 1, 2001 and December 31, 2014.
source: The initial incident fracture was defined as the first low-trauma fracture reported between January 1, 2001 and December 31, 2014.
evidence: This is the operational definition of the exposure variable.

claim: When more than one fracture occurred during a single event, only the fracture at the most proximal site was considered.
source: When more than one fracture occurred during a single event, only the fracture at the most proximal site was considered.
evidence: This is a methodological decision for handling multiple fractures.

claim: All fractures included in the analysis were radiologically ascertained.
source: All fractures included in the analysis were radiologically ascertained.
evidence: This describes the method of fracture ascertainment.

claim: Face, skull, finger, or toe fractures and high-trauma fractures due to traffic accidents were excluded.
source: Face, skull, finger, or toe fractures and high-trauma fractures due to traffic accidents were excluded.
evidence: This describes exclusion criteria for fracture types.

claim: The study participants were followed up to December 31, 2016 for mortality, allowing at least 2 years of follow-up post fracture.
source: The study participants were followed up to December 31, 2016 for mortality, allowing at least 2 years of follow-up post fracture.
evidence: This describes the follow-up period for the outcome.

claim: Skeletal age is operationally defined as the sum of the chronological age and the change in life expectancy associated with fracture.
source: Skeletal age is operationally defined as the sum of the chronological age and the change in life expectancy associated with fracture.
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the statistical analysis.

claim: A Cox's proportional hazards regression was used to quantify the association between an initial specific fracture and mortality.
source: For the first aim, a Cox's proportional hazards regression was used to quantify the association between an initial specific fracture and mortality, in which both fracture and confounding variables were analyzed in a time-dependent manner to minimize the risk of immortal time bias (Suissa, 2008).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: Both fracture and confounding variables were analyzed in a time-dependent manner to minimize the risk of immortal time bias.
source: For the first aim, a Cox's proportional hazards regression was used to quantify the association between an initial specific fracture and mortality, in which both fracture and confounding variables were analyzed in a time-dependent manner to minimize the risk of immortal time bias (Suissa, 2008).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to reduce bias, with citation.

claim: The models adjusted for confounding effects of age and severity of comorbidities.
source: The models adjusted for confounding effects of age and severity of comorbidities (Quan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the covariates included in the statistical models.

claim: Under the Gompertz law of mortality, the annual risk of dying associated with aging 1 year is remarkably consistent between ages 50 and 95 across ethnicities and over time.
source: Under the Gompertz law of mortality, the annual risk of dying associated with aging 1 year is remarkably consistent between ages 50 and 95 across ethnicities and over time (Brenner et al., 1993; Vaupel, 2010).
evidence: This is a property of the Gompertz law supported by citations.

claim: During the median follow-up period of 14 years, 95,372 men and 212,498 women had sustained a fracture.
source: During a median of 14 years of follow-up (interquartile range [IQR]: 6.5, 14.0 years), 95,372 men and 212,498 women had sustained a fracture.
evidence: This is a key result describing fracture incidence.

claim: The incidence of fractures was 10.9 fractures/1000 person-years (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.8, 11.0) in men and 23.2 fractures/1000 person-years (23.1, 23.3) in women.
source: The incidence of fractures was 10.9 fractures/1000 person-years (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.8, 11.0) in men and 23.2 fractures/1000 person-years (23.1, 23.3) in women.
evidence: This is a calculated incidence rate from the study data.

claim: Forearm, hip, and humerus fractures accounted for 55% of all fractures in men and 70% in women.
source: Collectively, forearm, hip, and humerus fractures accounted for 55% of all fractures in men and 70% in women.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Men and women with a fracture were on average older than those without a fracture.
source: As expected, men and women with a fracture were on average older than those without a fracture.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study data.

claim: Individuals with a fracture had more comorbidities than those who did not sustain a fracture.
source: Individuals with a fracture had more comorbidities than those who did not sustain a fracture (Table 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding shown in Table 1.

claim: The prevalence of myocardial infarction among patients with a fracture (9.3% in men and 4.7% in women) was higher than that among individuals without a fracture (4% in men and 1.5% in women).
source: For instance, the prevalence of myocardial infarction among patients with a fracture (9.3% in men and 4.7% in women) was higher than that among individuals without a fracture (4% in men and 1.5% in women).
evidence: This is a specific comparison of comorbidity prevalence.

claim: During a median follow-up of 6.5 years, 272,524 men and 277,194 women had died.
source: During a median follow-up of 6.5 years (6.0 years (IQR: 2.5, 10.0) in men, 6.7 years (3.3, 10.8) in women), 272,524 men and 277,194 women had died, yielding unadjusted mortality incidence rates of 6.55 deaths/100 person-years (95% CI: 6.48, 6.61) in men and 5.42 deaths/100 person-years (5.39, 5.46) in women.
evidence: This is a key result describing mortality incidence.

claim: The unadjusted mortality incidence rates were 6.55 deaths/100 person-years (95% CI: 6.48, 6.61) in men and 5.42 deaths/100 person-years (5.39, 5.46) in women.
source: During a median follow-up of 6.5 years (6.0 years (IQR: 2.5, 10.0) in men, 6.7 years (3.3, 10.8) in women), 272,524 men and 277,194 women had died, yielding unadjusted mortality incidence rates of 6.55 deaths/100 person-years (95% CI: 6.48, 6.61) in men and 5.42 deaths/100 person-years (5.39, 5.46) in women.
evidence: This is a calculated mortality rate from the study data.

claim: The unadjusted rate of mortality among patients with a fracture (6.54/100 person-years in men and 5.42/100 person-years in women) was greater than among those without a fracture (2.56/100 person-years in men and 2.24/100 person-years in women).
source: More importantly, the unadjusted rate of mortality among patients with a fracture (6.54/100 person-years in men and 5.42/100 person-years in women) was greater than among those without a fracture (2.56/100 person-years in men and 2.24/100 person-years in women).
evidence: This is a comparison of mortality rates between fracture and non-fracture groups.

claim: Men and women with a fracture at the hip, pelvis, or vertebra had a much greater risk of mortality than other fractures.
source: Analysis by fracture site revealed that men and women with a fracture at the hip, pelvis, or vertebra had a much greater risk of mortality than other fractures (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from site-specific analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Individuals with any fragility fracture were associated with a 30–45% increased hazard of death (adjusted hazard ratio = 1.46 (95% CI: 1.45, 1.48) in men; 1.28 (1.27, 1.30) in women).
source: Individuals with any fragility fracture were associated with a 30–45% increased hazard of death (adjusted hazard ratio = 1.46 (95% CI: 1.45, 1.48) in men; 1.28 (1.27, 1.30) in women).
evidence: This is a key finding from the multivariable-adjusted Cox regression.

claim: Men and women with a hip or femur fracture had an almost twofold greater risk of death than those without a fracture, for the same age and comorbidity profile.
source: For the same age and comorbidity profile, men and women with a hip or femur fracture had an almost twofold greater risk of death than those without a fracture.
evidence: This is a specific finding about hip and femur fractures from the adjusted analysis.

claim: The increased risk of mortality was also observed among those with a proximal fracture, such as the pelvis, vertebrae, humerus, rib, clavicle, and lower leg fracture after controlling for age and comorbidities.
source: The increased risk of mortality was also observed among those with a proximal fracture, such as the pelvis, vertebrae, humerus, rib, clavicle, and lower leg fracture after controlling for age and comorbidities.
evidence: This is a finding about proximal fractures from the adjusted analysis.

claim: There was no significantly increased risk of death following a forearm, knee, ankle, hand, or foot fracture.
source: However, there was no significantly increased risk of death following a forearm, knee, ankle, hand, or foot fracture (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding about distal fractures shown in Figure 3.

claim: Patients with a fracture have lost years of life, and hence their skeletal age was greater than their chronological age.
source: Patients with a fracture - any fracture at all - have lost years of life, and hence their skeletal age was greater than their chronological age.
evidence: This is a key finding about skeletal age.

claim: For a given age, men with a fracture on average had greater skeletal age than women by approximately 1 year.
source: For a given age, men with a fracture on average had greater skeletal age than women by approximately 1 year.
evidence: This is a sex-specific finding about skeletal age.

claim: The loss of years of life was more pronounced in younger age groups and gradually converged in the older age groups.
source: In either sex, the loss of years of life was more pronounced in younger age groups and gradually converged in the older age groups.
evidence: This is a finding about age-related patterns in years of life lost.

claim: Patients with a hip fracture had the highest skeletal age than those with other fractures.
source: As expected, patients with a hip fracture had the highest skeletal age than those with other fractures.
evidence: This is a comparative finding about hip fractures.

claim: A 70-year-old man who had sustained a hip fracture would have a skeletal age of 75 years (i.e. a loss of 5 years of life).
source: For example, a 70-year-old man who had sustained a hip fracture would have a skeletal age of 75 years (i.e. a loss of 5 years of life); however, if a 50-year-old man with a hip fracture would have a skeletal age of 56.8 years which is equivalent to almost 7 years of life lost.
evidence: This is a specific example calculation of skeletal age.

claim: A 50-year-old man with a hip fracture would have a skeletal age of 56.8 years which is equivalent to almost 7 years of life lost.
source: For example, a 70-year-old man who had sustained a hip fracture would have a skeletal age of 75 years (i.e. a loss of 5 years of life); however, if a 50-year-old man with a hip fracture would have a skeletal age of 56.8 years which is equivalent to almost 7 years of life lost.
evidence: This is a specific example calculation of skeletal age.

claim: Fractures at the femur, pelvis, vertebrae, and humerus signified a significant loss of years of life (around 5 years).
source: Other fractures such as the femur, pelvis, vertebrae, and humerus also signified a significant loss of years of life (around 5 years); thus, 50-year-old patients with one of these fractures are estimated to have a skeletal age of around 55 years.
evidence: This is a finding about years of life lost for specific fracture types.

claim: 50-year-old patients with femur, pelvis, vertebrae, or humerus fractures are estimated to have a skeletal age of around 55 years.
source: Other fractures such as the femur, pelvis, vertebrae, and humerus also signified a significant loss of years of life (around 5 years); thus, 50-year-old patients with one of these fractures are estimated to have a skeletal age of around 55 years.
evidence: This is a specific example calculation of skeletal age.

claim: Fractures at the rib, clavicle, and lower leg were associated with lower years of life lost.
source: However, fractures are the rib, clavicle, and lower leg were associated with lower years of life lost, and the skeletal age of patients with one of these fractures was generally lower than patients with a more serious fracture (e.g. hip fracture).
evidence: This is a comparative finding about less severe fractures.

claim: A 60-year-old patient with a lower leg fracture would be expected to have a skeletal age of 62.4 years for men or 61.9 years for women.
source: For instance, a 60-year-old patient with a lower leg fracture would be expected to have a skeletal age of 62.4 years for men or 61.9 years for women (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a specific example calculation of skeletal age.

claim: The magnitude of the association between individual sites of fracture observed in this study is slightly lower than that documented in several previous cohort studies.
source: However, the magnitude of the association between individual sites of fracture observed in our study is slightly lower than that documented in several previous cohort studies (Bliuc et al., 2009; Browner et al., 1996; Melton et al., 2013; Haentjens et al., 2010; Tran et al., 2017), with hip fractures being associated with a 1.7-to-6-fold increased risk of death (Haentjens et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: Hip fractures have been associated with a 1.7-to-6-fold increased risk of death in previous studies.
source: However, the magnitude of the association between individual sites of fracture observed in our study is slightly lower than that documented in several previous cohort studies (Bliuc et al., 2009; Browner et al., 1996; Melton et al., 2013; Haentjens et al., 2010; Tran et al., 2017), with hip fractures being associated with a 1.7-to-6-fold increased risk of death (Haentjens et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a range of effect sizes from previous literature.

claim: The discrepancy in effect size could be due to the difference in study populations.
source: This discrepancy could be due to the difference in study populations.
evidence: This is an explanation for differences with previous studies.

claim: Cohort studies usually recruit healthy participants.
source: While cohort studies usually recruit healthy participants, our national registry-based study was able to document all individuals in Denmark.
evidence: This is a characterization of typical cohort study design.

claim: The control group (those without a fracture) in this study included individuals in poor health conditions with multiple comorbidities who are usually unable to be recruited in a cohort study.
source: As a result, our control group (i.e. those without a fracture) included individuals in poor health conditions with multiple comorbidities who are usually unable to be recruited in a cohort study.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the study population differs from typical cohorts.

claim: Whether the association between fracture and mortality is causal or not is a matter of contention.
source: Whether the association between fracture and mortality is causal or not is a matter of contention.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about causality.

claim: It is commonly assumed that the association between fracture and mortality is confounded by comorbidities.
source: It is commonly assumed that the association is confounded by comorbidities, but multiple studies have found that comorbidities contributed little to the excess risk of mortality among fractured patients (Vestergaard et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a common assumption in the field.

claim: Multiple studies have found that comorbidities contributed little to the excess risk of mortality among fractured patients.
source: It is commonly assumed that the association is confounded by comorbidities, but multiple studies have found that comorbidities contributed little to the excess risk of mortality among fractured patients (Vestergaard et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The significant fracture-mortality association remained unchanged after adjusting for comorbidities in this study.
source: In the present analysis, we have also adjusted for comorbidities, and the significant fracture – mortality association remained unchanged, suggesting that the association is unlikely due to comorbidities.
evidence: This is a finding from the adjusted analysis.

claim: The association between fracture and mortality is unlikely due to comorbidities.
source: In the present analysis, we have also adjusted for comorbidities, and the significant fracture – mortality association remained unchanged, suggesting that the association is unlikely due to comorbidities.
evidence: This is an inference from the adjusted analysis results.

claim: Existing fracture risk assessment models such as Garvan and FRAX provide the estimated probability of fracture over a 10 year period without any information on mortality.
source: Existing fracture risk assessment models such as Garvan (Nguyen et al., 2007) and FRAX (Kanis et al., 2007) provide the estimated probability (i.e. absolute risk) of fracture over a 10 year period without any information on mortality.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing risk assessment tools with citations.

claim: Doctors and patients have difficulty in understanding and interpreting probability.
source: However, doctors and patients have difficulty in understanding and interpreting probability (Gigerenzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on risk comprehension.

claim: Conveying a low, though clinically significant absolute risk might provide a false peace of mind and underestimated risk perception, leading to increasing possibilities of refusing the recommended treatment.
source: Conveying a low, though clinically significant absolute risk (e.g. 'Your risk of hip fracture over the next 10 years is 5%') might provide a false peace of mind and underestimated risk perception, leading to increasing possibilities of refusing the recommended treatment (Trevena et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a concern about risk communication supported by citation.

claim: Poor communication about fracture risk and mortality consequences might have contributed to the global crisis of undertreatment of osteoporosis.
source: Thus, poor communication about fracture risk and mortality consequences might have contributed to the global crisis of undertreatment of osteoporosis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the cause of undertreatment.

claim: A natural frequency metric has been consistently shown to be easier and more friendly to doctors and patients than the probability-based metrics.
source: A natural frequency metric has been consistently shown to be easier and more friendly to doctors and patients than the probability-based metrics (Akl et al., 2011; Gigerenzer et al., 2007; Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on risk communication.

claim: Skeletal age can be used to convey the possible benefit of treatment, providing an alternative metric to the conventional metrics such as relative risk or relative risk reduction.
source: In addition, the skeletal age can be also used to convey the possible benefit of treatment, providing an alternative metric to the conventional metrics such as relative risk or relative risk reduction.
evidence: This is a proposed application of skeletal age.

claim: Zoledronic acid treatment reduced the risk of death by 28%.
source: For instance, a patient might find the statement 'Zoledronic acid treatment helps a patient with a hip fracture gain 3 years of life' much easier to understand and probably more persuasive than 'Zoledronic acid treatment reduced the risk of death by 28%' (Lyles et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited clinical trial.

claim: Heart age and lung age have been demonstrated to be superior to the conventional risk metrics.
source: Skeletal age is an addition to the already available metrics such as 'Heart Age,' 'Lung Age,' and more recently 'Covid Age' which have been demonstrated to be superior to the conventional risk metrics (Grover et al., 2007; Lowensteyn et al., 1998; Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015; Bonner et al., 2015; Svendsen et al., 2020) in terms of positive behavioral changes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on effective age metrics.

claim: Individuals who were given heart age had a greater smoking cessation rate compared with usual care.
source: For instance, compared with usual care, individuals who were given heart age had a greater smoking cessation rate (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015; Bonner et al., 2015), substantial improvement in weight, body mass index, and physical activity (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015), and a greater proportion of high-risk patients returning for a follow-up appointment (Lowensteyn et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on heart age interventions.

claim: Individuals given heart age showed substantial improvement in weight, body mass index, and physical activity.
source: For instance, compared with usual care, individuals who were given heart age had a greater smoking cessation rate (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015; Bonner et al., 2015), substantial improvement in weight, body mass index, and physical activity (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015), and a greater proportion of high-risk patients returning for a follow-up appointment (Lowensteyn et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on heart age interventions.

claim: The use of heart age led to a greater proportion of high-risk patients returning for a follow-up appointment.
source: For instance, compared with usual care, individuals who were given heart age had a greater smoking cessation rate (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015; Bonner et al., 2015), substantial improvement in weight, body mass index, and physical activity (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015), and a greater proportion of high-risk patients returning for a follow-up appointment (Lowensteyn et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on heart age interventions.

claim: The use of heart age led to significantly greater improvement at 12 months in metabolic parameters or lipid profiles.
source: The use of heart age also led to significantly greater improvement at 12 months in metabolic parameters (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2015) or lipid profiles (Grover et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on heart age interventions.

claim: A cluster randomized controlled trial in Norway found that heart age was a good way to communicate cardiovascular risk and to motivate individuals to reduce cardiovascular risk factors.
source: A recent cluster randomized controlled trial in Norway also found that heart age was a good way to communicate cardiovascular risk and to motivate individuals to reduce cardiovascular risk factors (Svendsen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited randomized controlled trial.

claim: The use of lung age could lead to a clinically significant increase in the reported smoking cessation rates.
source: Similarly, the use of lung age could also lead to a clinically significant increase in the reported smoking cessation rates (Kaminsky et al., 2011; Takagi et al., 2017; Parkes et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on lung age interventions.

claim: Effective age metrics can help patients better understand their risk and lead to preventive changes.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that effective age metrics can help patients better understand their risk and lead to preventive changes.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited evidence on effective age metrics.

claim: A web-based calculator 'BONEcheck.org' has been developed to assist healthcare professionals and the public to estimate the risk of fracture and skeletal age for an individual with specific risk profiles.
source: A web-based calculator 'BONEcheck.org' has been developed to assist healthcare professionals and the public to estimate the risk of fracture and skeletal age for an individual with specific risk profiles, potentially improving doctor-patient risk communication.
evidence: This describes a tool developed as part of this work.

claim: The study included a whole-country population with long follow-up and robust diagnostic data, minimizing potential selection bias and misclassification.
source: First, we included a whole-country population with long follow-up and robust diagnostic data, minimizing potential selection bias and misclassification (Frank, 2000), and allowing us to examine mortality risk following individual fracture sites.
evidence: This is a strength of the study design.

claim: The current study analyzed both fracture and covariates in a time-dependent manner, making it statistically rigorous in minimizing an immortal time bias.
source: Second, the current study analyzed both fracture and covariates, such as aging and the presence of comorbidities in a time-dependent manner, making it statistically rigorous in minimizing an immortal time bias and sufficiently accounting for confounding effects.
evidence: This is a strength of the statistical approach.

claim: The use of registry-based data is prone to variable data accuracy, the lack of specific clinical information, and non-medical factors.
source: However, the use of registry-based data, originally documented and coded for administrative or reimbursement purposes is prone to variable data accuracy, the lack of specific clinical information, and non-medical factors (Mazzali and Duca, 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation of registry-based studies cited from the literature.

claim: The Danish NHDR includes excellent, complete medical records and precise diagnoses for all individuals living in Denmark since 1995.
source: Fortunately, all essential study variables (i.e. comorbidities, fracture, and death) were systematically obtained from the Danish NHDR that includes excellent, complete medical records and precise diagnoses for all individuals living in Denmark since 1995 (Andersen et al., 1999; Vestergaard and Mosekilde, 2002).
evidence: This is a characterization of the data source supported by citations.

claim: The use of diagnosis-based comorbidities is possibly associated with lower sensitivity than the self-reported ones.
source: The use of diagnosis-based comorbidities, though possibly associated with lower sensitivity than the self-reported ones (Lujic et al., 2017) is able to capture the severe health disorders that prompt the participants to seek for medical assistance.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged with citation.

claim: Diagnosis-based comorbidities are able to capture the severe health disorders that prompt the participants to seek for medical assistance.

claim: Skeletal age combines the risk that an individual will sustain a fracture and the risk of mortality once a fracture has occurred.

claim: Skeletal age is expected to improve risk communication and ultimately improve treatment uptake among patients who are indicated for treatment.
